title: Portfolio Fort
principle: Allocation across asset classes; hedging and risk management
product: Asset allocation, multi-asset funds, protective puts
philosophy: Don't put all your eggs in one basket

lessons.title: Your mix: asset allocation
lessons.subtitle: How much in shares, how much in safety
lessons.capability: Choose a mix of shares and safer assets that fits a goal's timeline.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Shares grow fastest, right? So I'll put 100% in shares. Easy!

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Fastest on average, Dash. But some years they fall hard.
The real question is: how much in shares, and how much somewhere calmer? That split is your asset allocation.

steps.title: The mix dial
steps.caption: Turn the dial from all-FD to all-index-fund. Watch a typical year and a bad one.

predict.question: What happens to the bad years as you add more shares?
predict.reveal: More shares means more growth on average, and deeper bad years. Time is what lets you ride them out.

steps.question: Your goal is 2 years away. Which mix fits best?

options.text: Mostly safe, a little in shares
options.why: Right. Little time to recover from a bad year, so keep most of it calm.
A crash in year 2 could leave you short exactly when you need the money.
Safe from crashes, but The Melt eats it.

steps.question: Why do long goals usually hold more shares?

options.text: There's time to recover from bad years
options.why: Yes. Over 10+ years, shares have usually beaten safer options, despite the dips.
They can. Time makes recovery likely, not certain.
No rule says so. It's about time and risk.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Asset Allocation
steps.realLife: Multi-asset and balanced advantage funds in India manage a mix of shares, bonds and gold for you. A simple DIY version: an index fund plus a debt fund, in your chosen split.
steps.mission: Ask a parent: if they invest, roughly what share is in shares versus FDs or gold?
steps.deeper: A famous study of big pension funds found the asset mix explained most of how much their returns swung over time, far more than which shares they picked.

lessons.title: Fort Defense
lessons.subtitle: Every asset has a weakness
lessons.capability: Explain why a mix of assets survives more kinds of trouble than any single one.

steps.speaker: melt
lines: Hee hee. My fog is rolling in, and I've brought friends: Crash Goblins, Rate-Hike Golems, Surprise-Bill Bats…

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Every monster hits a different asset. Shares fall in crashes, bonds dip when rates rise, cash melts in the fog.
Build a fort that can face all of them.

steps.title: Defend Kip's fort
steps.caption: Place 5 towers, then face 5 waves. After each wave you may move one tower.

predict.question: Which fort survives the most waves?
predict.reveal: A mix. Each tower covers another's weakness. All-cash survives but barely grows; all-shares grows but often falls.

steps.question: Which tower beats the Surprise-Bill Bats?

options.why: Yes. Bills need money you can reach today.
Shares might be down when the bill arrives.
Bonds help, but selling takes time and the price may be low.

steps.question: Why does a mixed fort hold up better?

options.text: Its assets don't all fall at once
options.why: Right. When shares crash, gold and bonds often hold. That's diversification across asset classes.
Not in boom years. It wins by surviving everything.
They attack everyone. A mix just takes less damage.

steps.title: In real life
steps.realLife: In 2008 and in March 2020, Indian shares fell over 35% in a few months while gold rose. People holding both fell far less than people holding only shares.
steps.deeper: Correlation measures how much two assets move together. Diversification only helps with assets that don't move in lockstep. In a panic, many risky assets fall together, which is why safe assets matter.

lessons.title: Rebalancing
lessons.subtitle: Sell high, buy low, by rule
lessons.capability: Explain rebalancing and why it makes you sell high and buy low.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: My shares went up 30%! Now they're most of my money. That's good, right?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: It feels good. But your plan was 50/50, and now you're taking more risk than you chose.
Rebalancing means moving money back to your plan, usually once a year.

steps.title: Boom, then crash
steps.caption: Play two years. After the boom, choose: rebalance or leave it?

predict.question: After a boom, rebalancing means you…
predict.reveal: You sell some of what rose and buy what lagged. It's a rule that makes you sell high and buy low.

steps.title: Rebalance Rush
steps.caption: Six market years. After each one you have 10 seconds to get back to 60/30/10.

steps.question: Your 50/50 plan drifted to 70% shares. Rebalancing means…

options.text: Selling some shares to get back to 50/50
options.why: Right. Back to the risk you chose.
That's chasing performance: more risk, not less.
That's quitting the plan, not rebalancing.

options.text: Once a year, or when the mix drifts a lot
options.why: Yes. Often enough to control risk, rarely enough to keep costs and taxes low.
Costs and taxes would eat you alive.
Then a boom quietly turns a calm plan into a risky one.

steps.title: In real life
steps.realLife: Many investors rebalance on a fixed date, like their birthday. You can also rebalance by sending new SIP money to whatever is below target, which avoids selling.
steps.deeper: In India, selling equity held under a year triggers short-term capital gains tax, so many investors rebalance with new money first, or after the one-year mark.

lessons.title: Hedging: insurance for investments
lessons.subtitle: Pay a little to avoid losing a lot
lessons.capability: Explain a hedge as insurance: a small cost that limits a big loss.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: I'm scared of a crash, Kip. Should I just sell everything?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: There's a middle way: a hedge. It's like insurance on your investments.
You pay a small price, and if things crash, the hedge pays out.

steps.title: Crash insurance
steps.caption: Try each year, insured and not. Is the insurance worth it?

options.why: Yes. A small, certain cost to avoid a big, uncertain loss.
A lottery ticket is a gamble. A hedge reduces risk.
Hedges always cost something: a fee, or giving up some gain.

steps.question: In a good year, the insured investor…

options.text: Gains a bit less, because of the cost
options.why: Right. Like health insurance in a healthy year: you paid, and that's fine.
The insurance only costs ₹300.
The cost comes off the gain.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Hedge + Futures & Options
steps.realLife: A put option gives you the right to sell at a set price: a floor under your shares. Futures and options trade on the NSE. A SEBI study found about 9 in 10 individuals who traded them lost money, mostly by speculating rather than hedging.
steps.deeper: Hedging with puts is how many big funds protect a portfolio. For most individuals, a sensible asset mix and an emergency fund are cheaper hedges.

lessons.title: Boss: Fortress Siege
lessons.subtitle: Eight waves. One fort.
lessons.capability: Build and rebalance a mixed portfolio through many kinds of market trouble.

steps.speaker: melt
lines: The final siege! Eight waves, every monster I have. Let's see your fort melt.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Mix your towers, keep a cash gate, and rebalance after each wave. We've got this.

steps.title: Fortress Siege
steps.caption: Eight waves. Survive them all and grow.

steps.brief: Siege run! Spread your coins across SAFE, BALANCED and WILD, and keep cash for surprises.

steps.question: The best defence against unknown market monsters?

options.why: Yes. You can't predict the next wave, so be ready for all of them.
Nobody can, reliably.
Every asset has a weakness.

steps.question: What does a hedge cost you in good years?

options.why: Right. That's the price of protection.
There's always a cost.
Only the premium.

steps.title: World complete: Portfolio Fort
steps.realLife: You can now build a mix that fits a goal, keep it on plan with rebalancing, and explain hedging as insurance. That's how professional portfolios are run.
